title: W0299 `borrow_projection_copy` IS SILENT WHEN A BORROW PROJECTION IS PASSED TO A USER CALLEE THAT KEEPS IT -- `keep(w.r, mut v)`, a storing associated function and `k.put(w.r)` each copy the field and run its `Drop` body twice on every surface, and none of them warns; the lint fires only for the `Vec.push` builtin argument and a TRAIT associated-function argument. design.md now says which call copies (d618ccbcf), so the rule to implement is settled
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-09-14-10 at its close. That row's open question was whether the discard-elision should exist; Gowtham decided on 2026-09-26 to keep it, and d618ccbcf documents it in design.md § "Field projection off a borrow". What remains is the lint: it should warn exactly when the callee keeps the argument, and today it misses every user callee that does.

The measurement is B-2026-09-14-10's 2026-09-17 table (Group B, x86_64 Linux at f1cf626), with `karac check` per cell:

    cell                              copies?   warns?
    consume(w.r)   free, discards      no        no      correct
    v.push(w.r)    builtin, stores     YES       YES     correct
    keep(w.r,..)   free, stores        YES       no      MISSED
    Sk.take(w.r)   assoc, discards     no        no      correct
    k.put(w.r)     method, stores      YES       no      MISSED
    let m = w.r    let initializer     YES       YES     correct (control)

The same table also needs a storing ASSOCIATED function, which was not measured there.

WHY IT IS MISSED, from that note: the user-method-argument warning sits in `dispatch_trait_assoc_fn` (the trait associated-function path), which an inherent `impl K { fn put(mut ref self, x: R) }` call never reaches, and a free-function argument has no warning site at all. The blocker the row recorded is that the call site has the parameter TYPE but not the callee's AST `Function`, which `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` needs to answer "does the callee keep it". Codegen already answers that question to decide whether to copy, so the lint and the copy should ask the same predicate rather than two that can drift.

title: `for g in v.into_iter()` DOES NOT CONSUME `v` OR MOVE ITS ELEMENTS, ON ALL FOUR SURFACES -- the element's `Drop` body runs after the loop instead of at the end of each iteration, TWICE when the loop moves `g` on (`let h = g`, `w.push(g)`), BEFORE the loop body reads the element when the iterator is bound first (`let it = v.into_iter(); for g in it`), and `v.len()` after the loop still compiles and prints 2, where design.md says `into_iter()` consumes the collection
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while scoping B-2026-09-27-69, whose copy warning deliberately does not steer to `.into_iter()` because of this row. Measured 2026-09-27 on 1d152cc9e on `--interp`, JIT, `-O2` seq and `-O2` par, all four agreeing in every cell, valgrind 0 errors at -O0. Prefix: `struct D { id: i64, name: String }` with `impl Drop for D` printing `dD{id}{name}`, `fn mkd(n: i64) -> D` (name `n{n}`), `let v = vec![mkd(1), mkd(2)];`. design.md § Iteration: "`into_iter()` consumes it -- the caller cannot use the collection afterward", and § `for` loops: "To consume a collection while iterating, call `.into_iter()` explicitly (returns an owning iterator)". CELLS (got / owed): (1) `for g in v.into_iter() { println(f"g{g.id}"); } println("end")` prints `g1 g2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end`, owes `g1 dD1n1 g2 dD2n2 end` (each owned element dies at the end of its iteration). (2) `for g in v.into_iter() { let h = g; println(f"h{h.id}"); }` prints `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end`, owes `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 end`: `h` runs each body and the iterator runs them all again. (3) `let mut w: Vec[D] = Vec.new(); for g in v.into_iter() { w.push(g); } println(f"l{w.len()}")` prints `dD1n1 dD2n2 l2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end`, owes `l2 end dD1n1 dD2n2`: the iterator runs the bodies of elements `w` now owns. (4) `let it = v.into_iter(); for g in it { println(f"g{g.id}"); }` prints `dD1n1 dD2n2 g1 g2 end`: both bodies run BEFORE the loop reads either element, so the loop reads values already destroyed. (5) `for g in v.into_iter() { println(f"g{g.id}"); } println(f"len{v.len()}")` compiles and prints `len2` after the bodies ran; it owes a use-after-move error. A bare `for g in v` is the other spelling and is correct by design: it borrows `v`, and moving `g` out is the documented copy, now reported by W0299 (B-2026-09-27-69). The loop over a TEMPORARY, which already owns its elements and is where a consuming `.into_iter()` over a local would naturally route, is wrong the other way (same four surfaces, same agreement, with `fn mkv() -> Vec[D] { vec![mkd(1), mkd(2)] }`): (6) `for g in mkv() { println(f"g{g.id}"); } println("end")` prints `g1 g2 end` and never runs either body, owes `g1 dD1n1 g2 dD2n2 end`; (7) `for g in mkv() { if g.id == 1 { break; } }` prints `end`, owes `dD1n1 dD2n2 end`. Moving the element on is right there (`let h = g` prints `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 end`), so the owning loop drops what it moves and loses what it keeps. The faults split four ways (the fourth is cells 6-7): the ownership checker does not mark `v` moved by `.into_iter()` (cell 5); the loop does not treat the element as owned, so nothing drops it per iteration and moving it on does not disarm the iterator's drop (cells 1-3); and a bound iterator drops its elements early (cell 4).

WIDENED 2026-09-30 by B-2026-09-29-107's fix (1b4b37092): a `Vec[D]` DESTRUCTURED out of the element is the same fault one level down. `for pair in v.into_iter() { let (a, j) = pair; let b = a; println(f"{j} {b.len()}") }` over `Vec[(Vec[D], i64)]` crashed on every compiled surface before that fix (valgrind 10); it is now memory-clean and prints `1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 dD1 dD2 x` compiled against `--interp`'s `1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 x` -- the leaf is a loop borrow, so `b` runs a copy's bodies and the collection runs them again, which is cell (2) here. The pattern spelling `for (a, j) in v.into_iter() { let b = a; .. }` and `out.push(a)` measure the same way. Unlike cells (1)-(3), `--interp` is right for these (it runs each body once, per iteration), so they are a run-vs-build split rather than an agreed fault.

UPDATE 2026-09-30, B-2026-09-29-109's fix: `--interp` now agrees with compiled on the DESTRUCTURE cells of the WIDENED note above. The interpreter treats an `.into_iter()` loop as lending its elements, as every compiled surface does, so a destructured leaf is a view there too. `for pair in v.into_iter() { let (a, j) = pair; let b = a; .. }` now prints `1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 dD1 dD2 x` on all four surfaces, where the note recorded `--interp` as the right one. The destructure-only cell, `for pair in v.into_iter() { let (a, j) = pair; .. }` over `Vec[(D, i64)]`, used to run each body twice on `--interp` alone; it now prints one body per element at the loop's end, the same as compiled. Both are this row's fault (`into_iter()` consumes nowhere), and a fix here changes the two backends together.

title: THE `borrow_projection_copy` LINT (W0299) IS STILL SILENT WHEN A BORROWED VALUE IS HANDED TO A KEEPING FREE-FUNCTION CALLEE -- `for g in v { let o = f(g); }` and `fn k(s: ref S) { let o = f(s.r); }` over `fn f(x: D) -> D { x }` copy the value and run its `Drop` body twice with no warning, where `let h = g` and `let o = s.r` now warn
detail: SOURCE NOTE: remainder of B-2026-09-27-69, whose fix (1d152cc9e) extends W0299 to a bare `for` element but keeps the lint's documented exemption for free-function arguments. That exemption was written for a DISCARDING callee: design.md § borrow_projection_copy measured `eat(s.r)` minting no copy and running the body once, which is still true (`for g in v { eat(g) }` prints each body once). A KEEPING callee is the case the exemption gets wrong. Measured 2026-09-27 on 1d152cc9e on `--interp`, JIT, `-O2` seq and `-O2` par, all four agreeing, valgrind 0: with `struct D { id: i64, name: String }` and `impl Drop for D` printing `dD{id}{name}`, `let v = vec![mkd(1), mkd(2)]; for g in v { let o = f(g); println("o"); } println("end")` prints `dD1n1 o dD2n2 o dD1n1 dD2n2 end` and `karac check` reports nothing. With `struct D { id: i64 }`, `struct S { r: D }` and `fn k(s: ref S) { let o = f(s.r); println(f"o{o.id}"); }`, `k(s)` prints `o1 dD1 dD1 end`, also with no diagnostic. Both runs match design.md's copy semantics, so the only gap is the warning. Telling the two cases apart needs the callee's keep/discard answer (does it return or store the parameter?), which the typechecker does not have today; ownership's `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` / `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` family answers it for codegen.

title: `partial_move_of_drop_enum` MISSES A PAYLOAD MOVED INTO A PRELUDE CONSTRUCTOR -- `match e { E.A(r) => { return Some(r); } ... }` and `let x = Some(r); return x;` over an `enum E` with its own `impl Drop` compile without the error that `E.A(r) => { return r; }` gets, and the backends then disagree about the enum's body: `--interp` prints no `dE` and jit / `-O0` / `-O2` print it once per call. The lint asks `binding_only_borrowed_with`, which reads the bare `Some(..)` callee as an entry-copying free function, so `r` looks borrowed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the same misreading B-2026-09-17-24's fix (9a60158b3) corrected in
`result_escape` for the codegen escape questions: a capitalized bare callee
(`Some`, `Ok`, `Err`) is a constructor, and its arguments are TRANSFERS. That
fix deliberately left the other `consume_class` callers unchanged, and this
lint (src/typechecker/items.rs, the `partial_move_of_drop_enum` emission) is
one of them.

    struct R { name: String }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn f1(e: E) -> Option[R] { match e { E.A(r) => { return Some(r); } E.B => { return None; } } }
    fn f2(e: E) -> Option[R] { match e { E.A(r) => { let x = Some(r); return x; } E.B => { return None; } } }
    fn f3(e: E) -> R { match e { E.A(r) => { return r; } E.B => { return R { name: f"z" }; } } }

        karac check : error[partial_move_of_drop_enum] on f3's pattern ONLY

    with f3 removed and main printing both results' names:

        karac run --interp  :  a b
        karac run (JIT)     :  dE dE a b
        karac build -O0/-O2 :  dE dE a b
        valgrind -O0        :  12 allocs / 12 frees, clean

design.md § Part 8 `Drop` rejects moving a payload out of an enum with its own
`impl Drop`; f1 and f2 are that move, so both should be the same error f3
gets. Unflagged, the two backends pick different answers for whether `E`'s
body runs over the moved-from value.

Measured 2026-09-28 at 1e1a6c9 plus B-2026-09-17-26's fix, which does not touch
the typechecker.

title: A growth-heavy `Map[i64, i64]` workload runs 1.63x Rust's `HashMap` at equal hashing (SipHash-1-3 both), and ties a plain C linear-probing table: kata:325's bench, 857.5 ms against 520.6 for rust_ovf
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-02 on the 4-core x86-64 container, karac 0.1.0-dev.10181+gf2907d370, kata:325 `bench/max_sub_len.kara` (kara-katas `leetcode/301-400/325-maximum-size-subarray-sum-equals-k`). Workload: 60 scans of a 200,000-value array, each scan building a FRESH `Map[i64, i64]` of prefix sums with `get` plus `entry(p).or_insert(i)`; the three arrays give a few hundred, tens of thousands, and ~200,000 distinct keys, so most of the time goes to maps that grow 16 -> 262144 buckets on every call. bench.sh, 30 runs: kara 857.5 ms ± 23.6; rust -O 524.2; rust_ovf 520.6; go 662.0; c clang -O3 802.2 (a hand-written linear-probing table, 75% load, doubling, SipHash-1-3 over the key, i.e. kara's runtime design minus the control-byte tag); python 2110. All sinks `343512294`. So the gap is to hashbrown's design, not to the compiler's code around the map: the C table of kara's shape is within 7%. CALLGRIND (kara, 6.64 G Ir; rust 4.04 G; c 3.42 G): `karac_hash_word` 3.06 G self over 32,862,060 calls = 93 Ir a hash, 46% of the program; erased resize 1.29 G over 660 resizes (rust's `reserve_rehash` 0.64 G); mono `karac_map_i64_i64_get` 154 Ir a call inclusive; the erased `karac_map_entry` path 259 Ir a call inclusive (12,000,000 calls). System time is 2x rust's (120.7 vs 63.7 ms), consistent with the per-call tables being freshly faulted in. WHAT WAS TRIED: a mono `karac_map_<K>_<V>_entry` (insert_old's inline byte-walk probe minus the value store, wired at entry_chains.rs's claim) cut the per-call instruction path but ran SLOWER, 898.2 ms against 850.1 in the same hyperfine session, which fits B-2026-09-09-12's finding that the byte walk loses to the runtime's SWAR group scan on mispredicts. Not shipped; the patch is kept at kata-patches/mono_entry_proto.patch in the project folder. OPEN QUESTION for whoever owns Map performance: is 1.63x on a growth-heavy workload expected next to B-2026-09-07-53's projected 1.27x on kata:146 (a steady-size map), or a regression? The two biggest levers measured here are the hash (93 Ir, not inlinable because the hasher is a construction-time choice, B-2026-08-22-27) and resize.

fix: 83cbad997f. The title's premise is legacy's: on v2, `for tok in s.split(",")` already walks a lazy StrSplit whose items are views, so no token allocates. The v2 cost was two runtime calls per token. The step found the separator through karac_mir_str_find, which built a StrSearcher per call (22% of the profile), and cut the piece through karac_mir_str_view, which ran its bytes through String::from_utf8_lossy (26%). Now a one-byte separator is scanned for in line (a one-byte needle is ASCII, so a matching byte never sits inside a char), and `slice` cuts a view in line whenever its clamped ends fall on char boundaries. A longer separator, or a cut inside a char, still goes to the runtime. Kata 331: 12.76G to 3.47G instructions and 0.96-1.07 s to 0.42-0.44 s, against legacy's 1.92 s and the row's Rust 434 ms. Guard test: tests/mir_build.rs mir_split_and_slice_cut_in_line (multi-byte separators, wide chars, slices out of range and inside a char; interpreter against -O0 and -O2), plus the same program on wasm32-wasip1.
title: (LEGACY PREMISE: on v2 the tokens were already views; the cost was two runtime calls a token, a StrSearcher build and a lossy re-borrow) `for tok in s.split(",")` heap-allocates and frees every token even when the loop only compares it, so kata 331's benchmark runs 5.3x Rust, 8.8x C and slower than CPython (2.31 s against 1.91 s)
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found benchmarking kata 331 (Verify Preorder Serialization), whose ★ arm is `for tok in preorder.split(",") { if slots == 0 { return false; } if tok == "#" { .. } else { .. } }` over strings of about 200,000 tokens. Measured on an x86-64 container, 30 runs each, karac built from main at bc22c5fe2 plus this thread's batch: Kāra 2.314 s, Rust `-O` 434 ms (`split(',')` iterates borrowed `&str`), C 262 ms (scans in place), Go 576 ms (`strings.Split` makes a slice of string headers that share the input's bytes), CPython 1.909 s. The sink matches in all five. callgrind on the Kāra binary: `karac_runtime_string_split` allocates each piece with its own `malloc(len)` + copy (runtime/src/lib.rs), and each element is freed through `karac_free_buf` when the temporary Vec drops, about 220 and 130 instructions per token respectively, out of about 520 per token in all (malloc, _int_malloc, malloc_consolidate, _int_free and free are over half the profile). Allocation count confirms it: one `malloc` per token plus the result buffer, and none for the iteration itself. The runtime already has a NON-OWNING String header (`{ptr, len, cap: 0}`, which the element drop skips; split uses it for empty pieces), so a split whose result cannot outlive its source could hand out views into the source. In `for t in s.split(sep)` the result is a temporary that dies with the loop while `s` lives on; what has to be proved is that `t` does not escape the body (no push, no store, no return, no move into a call that keeps it). Separately and cheaply, the scan compares a slice per byte position (`&hay[i..i+n] == needle`), where a one-byte separator could use `memchr`.

fix: 9abd7da4c8, on v2 (the row's legacy measurements predate M3). Before, every hashed-table lookup called karac_mir_map_find_hv: the probe ran through the key's `eq` glue, then the entry's index was counted through the Fenwick tree a holed table keeps, and karac_mir_map_at turned the index back into a pointer. That cost 62 instructions a lookup on kata 340, and `len()` was a call too. Now `MirMap` is `#[repr(C)]` with a six-word header (buf, entry_size, slots, holes, cells, ncells), and integer, `char` and `bool` keys are probed in line over the index. Every lookup hands back the entry pointer, so nothing counts an index: other keys use karac_mir_map_lookup_hv (or _lookup for a sorted table), and remove names the entry (karac_mir_map_remove_entry), which also drops the row's second hash on `remove`. `len()` and the walk of a hole-free table read the header in line. Kata 340: 5.59G to 3.93G instructions and 0.57-0.61 s to 0.39-0.49 s, against legacy's 3.61G and 0.39-0.46 s. Rust is not re-measured, since the Rust comparison is deferred until after M4. The remainder against Rust (the 93-instruction word hash, and karac_mir_map_remove_entry at about 200 instructions a call from Fenwick upkeep) is B-2026-10-24-6. Guard test: tests/mir_build.rs mir_table_lookups_agree_through_holes (holes, compaction, walks after removals, entry, get_or, indexing, set algebra, String keys, a sorted map; interpreter against -O0 and -O2), plus the same program on wasm32-wasip1.
title: AFTER B-2026-10-04-56 KATA 340'S `Map[char, i64]` BENCH STILL RUNS 1.85x RUST AT EQUAL HASHING (399 ms vs 216): each hash costs 92 instructions against Rust's ~74, the erased `remove` path hashes a key the `get` before it already hashed, and the mono insert costs ~70 instructions a call beyond its hash
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-04 on the x86-64 container, after the call-site hash landed: kara 3.43 G instructions (karac_hash_int 1.49 G over 16.2M calls, 92 Ir a call; main 0.79 G; karac_map_i32_i64_insert_old 0.70 G over ~10M calls; the erased remove path's KaracMap::lookup 0.26 G plus karac_map_remove_old 0.13 G), against rust -O's 1.98 G in all. THREE LEVERS, none tried yet. (1) The per-hash cost: karac_hash_int saves two registers and calls a cold init path from its entry (`push r14; push rbx` before the INIT check), and carries the nbytes clamp and branch; Rust inlines SipHash-1-3 into the probe. (2) `Map.remove` goes through the erased `karac_map_remove_old`, which hashes through the stored fn again, so the shrink step's `get(d)` then `remove(d)` is still two hashes; a mono remove taking the call-site hash would share it the way get and insert now do. (3) The mono insert body walks control bytes one at a time; B-2026-09-09-12's group scan only serves i64-key gets. SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-04-56, split out when that row closed.

title: The MIR borrow checker keeps a `Vec[(ref Node, i64)]` borrowed for as long as a `ref Node` copied out of one of its elements is live: `let (a, n) = v[0]; v.pop(); a.val` is refused on both MIR backends ("mutable borrow of _2 while it is borrowed", E0516), though core-semantics §1.1 makes the tuple `Copy` and the copied reference keeps the origin of the node, not of the vector; the same read out of a `Vec[ref Node]` runs, and `karac check` passes both

A one-integer f-string `f"{n}"` still runs about 3x legacy on the v2 compiled backend after B-2026-10-13-20's fix: 44M `f"{i % 7}"` take 0.86 s on `karac build --mir` against 0.28 to 0.31 s on legacy `karac build`, and kata 504's bench 1.97 to 2.25 s against 1.51 to 1.62 s
detail: Measured with a release karac at 5a4a35bb58 on a shared 4-core container, min of 5 runs. Program: B-2026-10-13-20's `fn main() { let mut total = 0; for i in 0..44000000 { let s = f"{i % 7}"; total += s.len(); } println(f"{total}"); }`. WHAT IS LEFT (read in the optimized IR, not profiled): per iteration one call to `karac_mir_string_of_i64(out, v)`, which mallocs the digits' block, then the String's drop frees it. No thread-local access is left on this path. How legacy gets to 0.3 s was not read; a guess is that its lowering is visible to LLVM, which can then drop an allocation whose only use is `len()`. A digit-count-then-inline-write lowering in codegen would make the same thing possible here. SOURCE NOTE: remainder of B-2026-10-13-20 (closed by fdb1d5fc22 + 5a4a35bb58).

title: A bare list literal used only to be walked or read, `for step in [1, 9] { .. }` or `let steps = [1, 9]; steps[0] + steps[1]`, heap-allocates a `Vec` every time it is evaluated under `karac build --mir`, where legacy `karac build` keeps it on the stack (B-2026-10-02-70's fix): 1,000,008 allocations against 9 for a million evaluations, so kata 752's bench, which walks `[1, 9]` four times per visited lock setting, is 2.5x legacy
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: kata 752 (Open the Lock), its bench: kara-katas leetcode/701-800/752-open-the-lock/bench/open_lock.kara. The ★ arm's breadth-first search turns each of the four wheels both ways with `for step in [1, 9] { let next = at + ((digit + step) % 10 - digit) * place; .. }`, so the literal is evaluated four times per setting popped, some 14.5 million times over 3000 locks. Measured with a debug karac (`--features llvm`) and runtime archives built at kara 1a5c083e3a; the three src/ commits on main since (c287c03cec, e08f9131e9, 56a4cad109) do not touch literal or `for` lowering. Shared 4-core container, three runs each.

READ: design.md § List literals makes `[a, b, c]` a `Vec` unless the expected type says otherwise, so the allocation is the literal semantics and eliding it is an optimisation, not a fix to typing. Legacy elides it in `compile_for` (`try_compile_for_scalar_vec_literal`, B-2026-10-02-70): a non-empty `Vec` literal of scalars or scalar tuples used as the `for` iterable becomes an entry-block `[N x T]` alloca. v2 lowers the literal through `prefix_literal` / `array_literal` in src/mir/lower.rs (around lines 5109 and 5151) and the `for` around line 5340, and nothing turns a literal that is never moved, mutated or grown into stack storage. The remedy is a hypothesis: the legacy rule at the `for` iterable, or more generally a MIR pass that demotes a `Vec` local built from a literal and only read (indexed, `len`, iterated) to a fixed array.

RELATED: B-2026-10-02-70 (the legacy twin, fixed), B-2026-10-15-56 (the out-of-line `vec_alloc` cost; this row is about the number of allocations, which that does not cover), B-2026-10-18-51 (the pre-size pass and `for`).

title: A list literal whose FIRST element is a `ref T` of a `Copy` `T` is typed `Vec[ref T]` even where a `Vec[T]` is expected: `for p in v.iter() { let u: Vec[i64] = [p]; }` is refused with "expected 'Vec[i64]', found 'Vec[ref i64]'" by `karac check` and `karac __mir-run`, while `[1, p]`, `let a: Array[i64, 1] = [p]`, `w.push(p)`, `let x: i64 = p` and `S { x: p }` are all accepted
detail: core-semantics §5.10: "A `ref T` or `mut ref T` whose `T` is `Copy` is read as a `T` wherever a `T` is expected: an operator operand, an argument, a `let` with a `T` annotation, a field or element of a literal, a return value." Measured at a719a6d597 on a `Vec[i64]` walked with `for p in v.iter()`: refused are `let u: Vec[i64] = [p];` (7:27), `let a: Vec[i64] = [p, 1];`, and the assignment `st = [p];` to a `let mut st: Vec[i64]`, each with the same message from `karac check` and from `karac __mir-run` (exit 3, 'error[mir]: typecheck'). Accepted, and printing the right values under `__mir-run`: `[1, p]` (a literal first element fixes the element type at `i64` and `p` is then read as one), `let a: Array[i64, 1] = [p]` (so the Array path does take the expected type), `w.push(p)`, `let x: i64 = p`, a tuple `(p, x)` against `(i64, i64)`, a struct literal `S { x: p }`, and `return p` from a `-> i64` fn. So the Vec path seems to take its element type from the first element rather than from the expected `Vec[T]` (not traced). Legacy `karac run --interp` accepts all of them. Same family as B-2026-10-19-32 (a list literal not taking the expected type when it is a generic method's argument), a different site: there the literal is an argument, here it is a `let` initialiser or an assignment's right side. The kata's natural line is `let mut stack: Vec[i64] = [p];` in 851's quietest-first arm; it is written `[*p]` (the explicit read §5.10 allows) until this closes. SOURCE NOTE: found writing kata 851 (Loud and Rich).

title: Float Display breaks an exact tie between two equally short decimals away from zero, where Python's repr keeps the even last digit: -75455689800034.625 prints -75455689800034.63 on every v2 backend and in `--interp`, Python prints -75455689800034.62; library/core-types.md § Printing says only "the shortest digits that read back", so which of the two is unspecified
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found writing kara-katas apps/cli/mini_geographiclib (the real-world apps thread, 2026-10-23), where one polygon area out of 581 output lines differed in its last digit from the Python oracle while every intermediate matched bit for bit. Measured at 9e09409535: `println(f"{-76034228193651.2 + 578538393616.5771}")` prints -75455689800034.63 under __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and run --interp; `f"{x:.30}"` shows the value is exactly -75455689800034.625, so .62 and .63 both read back and are equally near. Rust's `{}` gives .63 too (the rendering is Rust's shortest-digits algorithm, which rounds the last digit half up). Python gives .62; over .125/.375/.625/.875 at that magnitude Python prints .12/.38/.62/.88 (half to even) and Kara .13/.38/.63/.88. Ties happen only where the value has few fraction bits (large magnitudes; 142 of 5847 sampled floats with at most 12 fraction bits), and both backends agree, so this is not an A/B fault: it is a spec question plus Python parity, which the spec already cites for the exponent rule ("as Python's repr does"). Either pin half-to-even in core-types.md (and implement it) or say the tie is unspecified. The app emulates Python's choice in its own fmt() using the exact `{x:.60}` expansion, listed in its source header and README. Owner: the review thread (spec conformance) for the decision.

title: (NOT SMALL, kata thread 2026-10-24: 3.4x on kata 951's tuple match of two Option[shared] params, 1.31 s vs 0.39 s for nested matches) A `match` on a tuple of handle locals (`match (top_left, top_right, bottom_left, bottom_right) { (Quad.Leaf(p), ..) => .. }`) counts each handle into a built tuple and releases the tuple after the match, although the arms only read discriminants and Copy payloads: kata 558's `intersect` pays four increments and four `drop.shared` calls per Split node for it, 8 of the 8 count sites its IR has left
detail: SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-14-9, measured 2026-10-23 on main b854ea64ad. The elaborated MIR of kata 558's `intersect` (corpus/katas/501-600/558-*/bench/quad_tree_or) builds `_30 = (move _31, move _32, move _33, move _34)` from `_31 = retain(_17)` .. `_34 = retain(_26)`, matches `_30` by its fields' discriminants and `bool` payloads, and ends with `drop(_30)`. The four sources stay alive and are used afterwards (`Quad.Split(top_left, ..)`), so `rc_pairs` cannot cancel the pairs, and `rc_borrow` applies only to handles read out of `ref` parameters. In the IR (KARAC_MIR_LL) that is the 4 `add i64 .., 1` and 4 `drop.shared Quad` calls left in `kara.intersect` on the Split/Split path. core-semantics §6.1 says using a handle aggregate as a value counts its handles; whether a tuple built only to be matched is a use as a value is the open question. A lowering that matches each element place directly (no tuple), or a pass that leaves the tuple's fields uncounted when the tuple is only read and its sources outlive it, would remove the counts. Inferred cost: small. Removing the other 8 sites (570645fbea) moved the full bench from 1.99-2.10 s to 1.97-2.05 s, within noise; v2 already beats legacy on this bench (1.97-2.05 s vs 2.46-2.74 s). MEASURED 2026-10-24 by the kata thread at 086f304909 (release, karac build --mir): kata 951 (Flip Equivalent Binary Trees), whose natural arm is `match (root1, root2) { (None, None) => true, (Some(a), Some(b)) => .., _ => false }` over two bare (borrowed under D5) `Option[TreeNode]` params of a `shared struct`. Every call clones each parameter into the scrutinee tuple (`clone.Option[shared TreeNode]`) and drops the tuple at the end (`drop.(Option, Option)`), two increment/decrement pairs per call on handles only read. Bench (50,000 rounds x 20 pairs of 100-node trees): tuple match 1.31 s median, 9.55 G instructions; the same function as nested matches 0.38-0.40 s, 3.79 G, no clone or drop left, identical output; Rust Rc<RefCell> with overflow checks 0.52 s, 5.25 G; C 0.37 s, 3.99 G. So on this shape the tuple counts make v2 3.4x slower than the nested spelling and 2.5x Rust, contradicting the 'Inferred cost: small' above, which held only for kata 558.

title: The v2 REPL's remaining legacy-only pieces: `%show` and `--auto-clone` / `%set auto-clone` refuse on v2, `:provide` does not check that the provider implements the resource's trait until the next cell, and the `:provide` construction program still replays every earlier cell
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split from B-2026-10-23-6 when its value snapshots landed (7e5765dd1b), which closed the replay of earlier cells for ordinary statement cells. After the in-line Map probe (9abd7da4c8), kata 340's sliding window still pays about 200 instructions per `remove` in karac_mir_map_remove_entry (Fenwick upkeep on a holed table, a rebuild on the first hole, and compactions) and 93 per word hash, against Rust's ~74, so v2 sits at legacy's 3.6-3.9G instructions where Rust -O ran 1.98G
detail: SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-04-79, measured 2026-10-24 at 9abd7da4c8 on the x86-64 container (callgrind, kata 340 bench longest_k_distinct): 3.93G instructions in all; karac.main 1.37G (in-line probes), karac_hash_word 1.23G over 13.2M calls (93 each), karac_mir_map_remove_entry 0.60G over 2.98M calls (200 each) plus its rebuild/compaction helpers 0.37G and 0.23G. Levers: (1) keep the Fenwick tree lazy, rebuilt only when an index is asked of a holed table (only walks ask since lookups hand back pointers), which needs care because concurrent readers share a table; (2) inline the word hash (SipHash-1-3 of one word) instead of calling karac_hash_word; (3) cheaper compaction thresholds for small tables. The Rust comparison is deferred until after M4 (Gowtham 10-13), so this is low.
